content: I realized I hadn't mentioned #general > IsoGraph: Graph library Discussion Thread here and I thought some people would probably want to take a look. Curious if others would be interested in helping build out / develop this approach.

Is the goal to be like Python's networkx? (or igraph/rustworkx/networkit/petgraph)
As in, a way to manipulate graphs and run a bunch of algos to analyze them (but not for proving theorems)
No? It's all about theorems, and it has many theorems proved. I'm confused what led you to that conclusion?

Alex Meiburg said:

I'm confused what led you to that conclusion?

Depending on which question you're responding to, the answer is either

Alex Meiburg said:

Also, I'd just like to comment that Aristotle helped a lot with the development.

(and most commits list Claude as a coauthor)

or

Alex Meiburg said:

It is also quite computationally oriented: it's finite graphs only, and every graph carries a FinEnum with it for performance purposes.
Oh, yes, it's AI-generated, no question there. (With a lot of precise direction from me about exactly which things I wanted proved)

I see the confusion now. Yeah, it's computationally oriented, but still oriented towards proofs. Like, one of the first things implemented was a verified algorithm for computing a generating set of a graph's automorphisms, so that you can easily prove that two graphs are isomorphic or not even for trickier cases, like pairs of strongly regular graphs.
